                    MOTION TO LODGE COMPLAINT BY THE

       Pursuant to Rule 212 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”), 18 C.F.R. § 385.212, the

Maryland Office of People’s Counsel (“OPC”) moves to lodge in the record of the above-

captioned proceeding the amended complaint that OPC filed against PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) and the PJM Transmission Owners in Maryland Office

of People’s Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL26-63-000.

       OPC is a party to this proceeding, having filed a timely doc-less motion to

intervene in Docket No. RM26-4-000 on November 10, 2025.1 The Commission

instituted this proceeding through an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

concerning the interconnection of large loads to the interstate transmission system,

including the appropriate allocation of the transmission costs caused by such loads. The

issues raised in OPC’s Complaint are common to, and may be relevant to the

Commission’s consideration of, the matters under review in this docket.

                                               1
        The OPC Complaint challenges PJM’s hybrid load-ratio share and solution-based

distribution factor (“DFAX”) transmission cost allocation methodology contained in

Schedule 12 of the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff as unjust and unreasonable

under section 206 of the Federal Power Act, insofar as that methodology socializes to

existing customers the costs of regional baseline transmission projects driven by data

center and other large-load growth. As such, the Complaint raises the same cost-

allocation and cost-causation questions as the matter of interconnection of large loads to

the interstate transmission system that the Commission is examining in this docket. 2

       Lodging the Complaint will ensure that the Commission and the participants in

this proceeding have the benefit of the analysis, evidence, and proposed remedies set

forth therein. OPC emphasizes however, that it does not, by this motion, seek to litigate

the merits of the Complaint in this docket; the Complaint is being adjudicated in Docket

No. EL26-63-000. OPC offers it here solely so that the record of this proceeding reflects

the closely related matters at issue.

       For the foregoing reasons, OPC respectfully requests that the Commission grant

this motion and lodge the Complaint in the record of Docket No. RM26-4-000.

                                       INTRODUCTION

        Over the next decade, Maryland customers will pay about $1.6 billion through

their electric bills in additional costs for transmission projects driven primarily by the

energy needs of data centers located outside of Maryland. These costs result from

PJM’s hybrid load-ratio share and solutions-based distribution factor (“DFAX”)

transmission cost allocation methodology for assigning transmission cost

responsibility across sub-regions or “zones” of PJM. 3 PJM’s hybrid methodology

broadly socializes to all customers costs that data centers, not existing customers, are

         OPC requests that the Commission process this complaint under its fast-track

procedures. Expedited action is essential to protect Maryland electric customers from

the affordability crisis they are currently experiencing from high energy bills,

including significant recent increases in capacity market costs, and the imminent

compounding of unjust costs with each successive PJM RTEP procurement window.

That compounding is exemplified by the PJM Board’s recent approval and

Commission filing of its selections for the 2025 RTEP Window 1, adding $839.4

million in capital cost responsibility to Marylanders for transmission enhancements. 9

inequitable impacts of PJM’s transmission cost allocation methodology on Maryland

ratepayers, parallel adverse impacts emanating from the same flawed PJM cost

allocation methodology are occurring in other states within the PJM footprint due to

data center load growth. 11

            Not only are transmission costs increasing on a rapid upward trajectory, but

state-level retail large-load tariffs fail to remedy and may exacerbate the misallocation

of transmission costs resulting from application of PJM’s hybrid transmission cost

allocation methodology. Moreover, recent utility filings with the Commission of

transmission security agreements (“TSAs”) with large-load customers—which are

often confidential, highly variable, and fail to protect existing customers—are

accelerating. 12 These agreements do not sufficiently address or remedy the infirmities

arising from use of the flawed PJM hybrid transmission cost allocation methodology,

as further described below and in the accompanying Affidavit; moreover, they carry

potential legal consequences that may prove difficult to unravel.

           Fast-track processing is necessary (i) to provide meaningful consumer relief

before these additional massive costs are allocated under the same defective “hybrid”

transmission cost allocation methodology, (ii) to address the gap in allocation of

transmission costs not remedied by state-level retail large-load retail tariffs, (iii) to

prevent acceptance of TSAs as a default, but inadequate, remedy, and (iv) to avoid or

minimize the collection of amounts subject to refund. To accomplish these objectives,

the Commission should direct PJM to answer the complaint within 15 days and should

grant the complaint on an expedited basis.



                                           BACKGROUND

           PJM’s cost allocation methodology is being applied to a new paradigm in

which it is demonstrably no longer appropriate. Under this new paradigm,

         a.       Accelerating national data center growth.

         Electricity consumption by U.S. data centers has accelerated at a striking pace,

Laboratory (“LBNL”) estimates that data center electricity consumption grew at

approximately 4 percent per year from 2010 to 2014, rose to 7 percent per year from

2014 to 2018, and then surged to 18 percent per year from 2018 to 2023. 19 Data

centers represented approximately 2 percent of total U.S. electricity demand in 2018.

LBNL projects that figure may rise to as high as 12 percent by 2028, with annual

energy consumption more than quintupling from less than 100 terawatt-hours

(“TWh”) to roughly 575 TWh. 20

         The accelerating rate of growth is expected to continue for the foreseeable

future. 21 Bloomberg NEF estimates that U.S. data center power demand will rise from

roughly 35 GW in 2024 to 78 GW by 2035, representing a doubling of load over the

next decade. 22 At the midpoint of LBNL’s projections, data center demand would

double in just the next four years. 23

        b.       PJM data center load growth concentration: the Virginia epicenter,

        Amidst national data center growth, Virginia stands as the epicenter. Virginia is

the largest data center market in the world, with data center meters serving roughly 50

customers across PJM’s Dominion Load-Serving Entity (“DOM-LSE”) zone. 25 As of

December 2024, data centers represented 3.6 GW of demand in the Dominion zone,

reflecting, since 2013, a 660 percent increase in megawatt-hour

consumption. 26 Dominion has received approximately 40,000 MW of capacity

requests in 2024 alone—more than double the zone’s current peak demand of 18,408

MW. 27 As a result, Dominion expects to see a more-than-30-percent increase in peak

demand from 2025 to 2030, rising from 24,271 MW to 31,939 MW. 28
